subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Lu Yu: The Sage of Tea
description: A quick, practical guide to Lu Yu: The Sage of Tea.

hook.text: Lu Yu wrote 'The Classic of Tea' around 760 CE—the world's first book entirely about tea. It transformed tea from drink to art.

buildup.text: Orphaned as a child and raised in a Buddhist monastery, Lu Yu spent decades studying tea cultivation and preparation.

discovery.text: His book covered water quality, utensils, leaf grades, correct boiling, and even the spiritual state of the brewer.

twist.text: After his death, Lu Yu was deified. Tea merchants placed his statue in their shops—pouring tea over it for luck.

climax.text: Lu Yu's work codified tea culture for 1,200+ years. Chinese, Japanese, and Korean tea traditions all reference his text.

punchline.text: One orphan, one book, twelve centuries of influence. Lu Yu made tea sacred.

quiz.question: What did Lu Yu write?
options: 'The Classic of Tea' — the first book entirely about tea, around 760 CE

details.summary: Lu Yu was an 8th-century Chinese scholar who wrote The Classic of Tea, the world's first comprehensive book about tea cultivation, preparation, and appreciation. He transformed tea from a medicinal drink into an art form and is revered as the Sage of Tea.
details.whyItMatters: Lu Yu's work codified tea culture and elevated it from a folk practice to a respected art, influencing every tea tradition that followed across Asia.
takeaways: Lu Yu authored The Classic of Tea in the Tang Dynasty era
He established standards for tea preparation and water quality
He is honored as the patron saint of tea across Chinese culture

faq.question: What topics does Lu Yu's Classic of Tea cover in its chapters?
faq.answer: The book covers tea plant botany, processing methods, ideal water sources, proper utensils, brewing techniques, drinking customs, growing regions, and simplified methods. It is organized into three scrolls with ten sections.

faq.question: How did Lu Yu's work influence tea culture beyond China?
faq.answer: Japanese monks who studied in Tang Dynasty China brought Lu Yu's principles home, shaping the Japanese tea ceremony. Korean and Vietnamese tea traditions also draw on his emphasis on water quality, utensils, and mindful preparation.
